Codex

**Yes—the relationship between the outline, the well, and the changes in depth is where this gets interesting.** You have considerably more freedom than simply choosing “round or polygonal.” For a distinctly Deco direction, I’d explore **symmetry, repeated setbacks, and a strong central focus**. The architectural precedent is something like [Paul Frankl’s *Skyscraper* furniture](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/482533); my proposed translation is to make those setbacks descend *into* the saucer. The image shows four original design studies: | Concept | What it explores | My read | |---|---|---| | **A** | Clipped corners outside; repeated angular terraces inside | Strongest overall Deco direction. The geometry repeats at different scales and depths. | | **B** | Rounded exterior; sharply stepped interior | Softer to handle, with an architectural interior. The contrast gives it personality. | | **C** | Stair-stepped perimeter; traditional round well | Strongest silhouette. The outline carries the character even with a cup sitting on it. | | **D** | Angular exterior; continuous faceted slope inside | Sculptural, but less specifically Deco. Faceting alone can feel broadly geometric. | A few design decisions matter more than simply adding corners: - **Depth has a rhythm.** Two shallow, deliberate drops can feel more architectural than one deep depression. Broad ledges give those changes room to register. - **Corners can soften without losing the shape.** Slightly rounding an angular outline retains its organization; rounding every transition into a continuous curve weakens the stepped effect. - **The shapes should relate.** Repeating the same clipped corners inward feels intentional. A circular well within a stepped perimeter creates a different, equally deliberate relationship. - **Imagine the cup in place.** It will hide much of the interior. Keep enough geometry visible around it for the saucer to retain its identity. **I’d develop A and C first:** A for the descending architecture; C for its silhouette. You could also combine C’s perimeter with one restrained interior step—but I’d keep the center quiet so the whole thing doesn’t become visually crowded.

[Image #1] Does this make sense? Basically we are playing on the original version of the curved saucer by using ziggurat-inspired reliefs, such that it's like we only have 4 steps to make it curved. Don't generatee anythign yet, but just get to htinking becuase I want you to make this in blender

Codex

Yes—**you’re approximating a curved saucer with a staircase-shaped depression.** The terraces become the actual shape of the saucer, giving it that inverted-ziggurat character. I’m reading your drawing as: - **Overall:** 4.75 × 4.75 × 0.75 inches. - **Interior:** centered, nested square terraces, symmetrical on all four sides. - **Depth:** four downward drops of 0.15 inches gives a 0.60-inch recess, leaving a **0.15-inch bottom**. - **Center:** a flat square seat for the cup. The most interesting decision is **the horizontal width of each step**: - **Equal widths and equal drops** create a stepped diagonal in section—an inverted pyramid. - **Wider terraces toward the center, narrower toward the rim** approximate a bowl that flattens at the bottom and steepens toward its edge. That second arrangement is closer to your idea of “only having four steps to make it curved.” We could preserve sharp square corners while letting the spacing suggest curvature. Two details I’ll carry into the Blender model: your “side view” is really a **cross-section through the center**; the intact outer wall would conceal that staircase from a straight side view. And I’m treating the top-view grid as layout marks—the finished surface would have **nested square boundaries**, rather than individual recessed grid cells. I’d start with a generous central seat and deliberate, visible terraces. The remaining proportion to settle is how much of the 4.75-inch width belongs to that seat versus the surrounding steps.

I used these **square dimensions**, with each level dropping **0.15 inches**: | Level | Length × width | Depth below rim | |---|---|---| | Outer edge | 4.75 × 4.75 in | 0 | | First recess | 4.25 × 4.25 in | 0.15 in | | Second recess | 3.85 × 3.85 in | 0.30 in | | Third recess | 3.25 × 3.25 in | 0.45 in | | Central seat | 2.35 × 2.35 in | 0.60 in | That makes the **horizontal ledge widths on each side**: **0.25-inch outer rim → 0.20 → 0.30 → 0.45 → central seat** I treated the rim separately, then widened the interior terraces toward the center to suggest the bottom of a bowl flattening out. Your **equidistant version**, keeping the same outer size and central seat, would have **0.30-inch ledges throughout**: **4.75 → 4.15 → 3.55 → 2.95 → 2.35 inches.** Equal spacing would give it a more regular architectural rhythm; the current spacing gives it a more bowl-like profile.
